chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
In Quebec, “co-ownership” covers two quite distinct realities: divided co-ownership (the classic condo) and undivided co-ownership. They look similar on the surface but differ profoundly on the legal, financial, and practical levels.

This guide compares the two to help you choose with full knowledge — because the difference has real consequences.

Informational content. Each chapter ends with a lined “My Notes” page.

chapters.title: Divided Co-ownership (the Classic Condo)
chapters.html:
Understanding the most common model.

In divided co-ownership, each unit has its own separate title of ownership and its own lot number. There is a syndicate, a declaration of co-ownership, common charges, and a contingency fund. You finance your unit with your own mortgage.

  • A separate title per unit: simpler to finance and resell.
  • Syndicate and contingency fund governed by law.
  • The most widespread and best-regulated model.
Émilie's tip

Divided co-ownership is generally simpler to finance and resell, because each unit has its own title. For a first purchase, it's often the most reassuring choice.

chapters.title: Undivided Co-ownership
chapters.html:
Understanding this particular model.

In undivided co-ownership, several people own ONE single building together, without division into separate lots: each holds a share of the whole and enjoys use of a portion according to an indivision agreement. There are no separate titles per unit.

  • Often a lower entry price for a given area.
  • More complex financing: sometimes a common mortgage or special conditions.
  • Rests on an indivision agreement among co-owners: its quality is crucial.
  • Resale is sometimes more limited (a smaller pool of buyers).
Émilie's tip

In undivided co-ownership, the indivision agreement is EVERYTHING: it settles who pays what, who decides, and how someone exits. Have it reviewed by a notary before you buy; a bad agreement can turn into a nightmare.

chapters.title: Choosing Well for Your Situation
chapters.objective: Weighing the benefits and the risks.
chapters.html:
Weighing the benefits and the risks.

  • Divided: simpler, more liquid, better regulated — often the default choice.
  • Undivided: sometimes more affordable, but more complex to finance and resell, and highly dependent on the agreement and the other co-owners.
  • In both cases: check the documents, finances, and rules before buying.

The right choice depends on your budget, your tolerance for complexity, and your time horizon.

Émilie's tip

Never choose undivided co-ownership just because it's cheaper up front. The lower price often reflects greater complexity and lower liquidity. Understand the trade-off before you sign.

chapters.title: Action Plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, in concrete terms.

This week

  1. Confirm the type of co-ownership of the unit you're considering.
  2. Gather the documents (declaration or agreement).

Within 30 days

  1. Have the declaration (divided) or the agreement (undivided) reviewed.
  2. Check the financing implications.

After that

  1. Choose with full knowledge, with Émilie and the notary.

chapters.title: Resources & Glossary
chapters.html:
• Divided co-ownership: the classic condo, a separate title per unit.
  • Undivided co-ownership: a share of a single building, without separate lots.
  • Indivision agreement: the arrangement governing rights and obligations in undivided co-ownership.
  • Contingency fund: collective savings (mainly in divided co-ownership).
  • Liquidity: ease of resale, generally better in divided co-ownership.
